newsitem.title: USA: Clinton issues "call to action" in State of Union.
newsitem.headline: Clinton issues "call to action" in State of Union.

text.p: Laying out his second-term goals in a State of the Union speech, President Bill Clinton on Tuesday issued a national "call to action" to improve education, balance the budget and reform campaign financing.

"We face no imminent threat, but we do have an enemy: The enemy of our time is inaction," Clinton said in remarks prepared for delivery before the joint houses of Congress and millions watching on television. "So tonight, I issue a call to action ... to prepare America for the 21st century."

He made improving American education the top priority of his second four years, appealing for a "national crusade" to raise education standards to a level competitive with other industrial nations and "ensure that Americans have the best education in the world."

Abroad, Clinton vowed anew to pursue an expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation by 1999 and a "stable partnership" with Russia, which opposes NATO expansion. A Madrid summit in July is to start the process toward including former communist states of Central Europe into NATO.

He also pledged to seek a "deeper dialogue" with China instead of isolating Beijing as some critics would like. He said he would go to China and President Jiang Zemin would visit the United States in pursuit of that goal.
He outlined an American role abroad far short of being the world's policeman but drawing the line against isolationism.

"America must continue to be an unrelenting force for peace -- from the Middle East to Haiti, from Northern Ireland, to Africa. Taking reasonable risks for peace keeps us from being drawn into far more costly conflicts later," he said.

While Clinton issued a new call for Democrats and Republicans who control Congress to work together, he denounced Republican efforts to amend the U.S. Constitution to require a balanced federal budget. The Senate was to begin debating the measure Wednesday.

"I believe it is unnecessary and unwise to adopt a balanced budget amendment that could cripple our country in time of crisis later on, and force unwanted results such as judges halting Social Security checks or increasing taxes," Clinton said.

The speech, expected to last about an hour, was a compilation of poll-tested themes from his 1996 re-election campaign. A year after he used the same setting to declare "the era of big government is over," his speech was thin on grand, large-scale initiatives -- in line with the country's perceived mood toward less government intrusion.

He went into the annual ritual in the chamber of the House of Representatives enjoying some of the highest public approval ratings of his presidency -- 63 percent -- in spite of a nagging controversy over how he and his Democratic Party raised money for last year's campaigns.

Trying to take the sting out of that issue and put pressure on the Republican-controlled Congress, he appealed anew for reform of how election campaigns are financed and set a specific date of July 4, the Independence Day holiday, for completing the work.
"You know and I know that delay will mean the death of reform," he said.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, was cautious on Clinton's challenge, saying it should first be determined what laws were violated last year. A team of FBI agents is investigating and congressional oversight hearings are planned.
"I don't see how you can decide what you need to do in terms of reform until you see how existing laws are being violated or abused," Lott told reporters before the speech.
Clinton was clearly hoping to make education his ticket into the history books.

He proposed $51 billion for education in the fiscal year starting Oct. 1, a 20 percent increase over current spending, to pay for education, training and tax cuts tied to education that are to be outlined in his budget blueprint to be sent to Capitol Hill for consideration on Thursday.
Under his education programme spending would rise to nearly $60 billion a year by 2002 even as other programmes are cut to balance the federal budget by that year.

His crusade involves a 10-point plan topped by setting up a programme in the next two years for national achievement tests in 4th grade reading and 8th grade math to ensure mastery of the basics. He would increase student access to the Internet.

The plan would also ensure high quality standards for teachers, make sure students can read on their own by the end of the 3rd grade, make schools safe, disciplined and drug-free, and modernise schools.
